notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • Magnetism is associated with magnetic fields and magnetic forces.
  • A magnet attracts certain materials such as iron, cobalt and nickel.
  • Every ordinary bar magnet has two poles: north and south.
  • Like magnetic poles repel.
  • Unlike magnetic poles attract.
  • Magnetic poles always occur in pairs in ordinary magnets.
  • Isolated magnetic monopoles have not been experimentally confirmed.
  • Cutting a bar magnet produces smaller magnets, each having north and south poles.
  • Magnetic force is a non-contact force.
  • The SI unit of magnetic flux density is tesla.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Like poles → Repel

Unlike poles → Attract

2. Magnetic Poles
  • Magnetic poles are regions where a magnet's effect is strongest.
  • The two poles are called north pole and south pole.
  • Magnetic force is strongest near the poles of a bar magnet.
  • A freely suspended magnet aligns approximately north-south.
  • The end pointing approximately north is called the north-seeking pole.
3. Magnetic Field
  • A magnetic field is the region in which magnetic forces can act.
  • Magnetic field is represented by B in many equations.
  • The SI unit of magnetic flux density B is tesla.
  • Magnetic fields are produced by magnets.
  • Moving electric charges also produce magnetic fields.
  • Electric currents therefore produce magnetic fields.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Moving Charge / Current → Magnetic Field

4. Magnetic Field Lines
  • Magnetic field lines are imaginary lines used to represent a magnetic field.
  • Outside a bar magnet, field lines are conventionally drawn from north pole to south pole.
  • Inside the magnet, field lines continue from south pole to north pole.
  • Therefore, magnetic field lines form closed loops.
  • Magnetic field lines never intersect.
  • Closely spaced field lines indicate a stronger magnetic field.
  • The tangent to a field line gives the local field direction.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Outside magnet → N to S

Inside magnet → S to N

5. Why Magnetic Field Lines Do Not Cross
  • At any point, magnetic field has one definite direction.
  • If field lines crossed, the field would have two directions at the same point.
  • Therefore, magnetic field lines cannot intersect.
6. Magnetic Flux
  • Magnetic flux measures the amount of magnetic field passing through a surface.
  • Magnetic flux is represented by Φ.
  • For a uniform field perpendicular to area, Φ = BA.
  • More generally, Φ = BA cosθ.
  • The SI unit of magnetic flux is weber.
  • One weber is abbreviated Wb.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Magnetic Flux → Weber

Magnetic Flux Density → Tesla

7. Tesla
  • Tesla is the SI unit of magnetic flux density.
  • Symbol is T.
  • The unit is named after Nikola Tesla.
  • 1 tesla = 1 weber per square metre.
📌 Remember

1 T = 1 Wb/m²

8. Weber
  • Weber is the SI unit of magnetic flux.
  • Symbol is Wb.
  • The unit is named after Wilhelm Eduard Weber.
  • Magnetic flux is important in electromagnetic induction.
9. Natural Magnets
  • Magnetite is a naturally occurring magnetic mineral.
  • Magnetite has the chemical formula Fe₃O₄.
  • Naturally magnetised magnetite is historically called lodestone.
  • Lodestone was used in early compasses.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Lodestone → Naturally magnetised magnetite

Magnetite → Fe₃O₄

10. Artificial Magnets
  • Artificial magnets are made by magnetising suitable materials.
  • They can be made in bar, horseshoe, ring and other shapes.
  • Artificial magnets may be permanent or temporary.
  • Permanent magnets retain magnetism for long periods.
  • Electromagnets retain strong magnetism mainly while current flows.
11. Permanent Magnet
  • Permanent magnets retain their magnetisation after the magnetising field is removed.
  • Hard magnetic materials are suitable for permanent magnets.
  • High retentivity helps a magnet retain magnetisation.
  • High coercivity helps resist demagnetisation.
  • Permanent magnets are used in speakers, small motors and measuring devices.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Permanent Magnet → High Retentivity + High Coercivity

12. Temporary Magnet
  • Temporary magnets lose most of their magnetism when the magnetising influence is removed.
  • Soft iron is a common material for temporary magnetic applications.
  • Temporary magnets are useful where magnetism must be switched on and off.
13. Electromagnet
  • An electromagnet produces a magnetic field using electric current.
  • A coil of wire is commonly wound around a soft-iron core.
  • Current through the coil magnetises the core.
  • Magnetic strength can be controlled by changing current.
  • Switching off current greatly reduces magnetism in a soft-iron-core electromagnet.
  • Electromagnets are used in relays, electric bells, cranes and motors.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Electromagnet → Current + Coil + Soft-Iron Core

14. Increasing Strength of an Electromagnet
  • Increase current through the coil.
  • Increase number of turns in the coil.
  • Use a suitable soft magnetic core such as soft iron.
  • Improve coil geometry and reduce magnetic leakage where appropriate.
📌 Remember

More Turns + More Current + Soft-Iron Core → Stronger Electromagnet

15. Why Soft Iron Is Used in Electromagnets
  • Soft iron is easily magnetised.
  • It has high magnetic permeability.
  • It has relatively low coercivity.
  • It loses most magnetism when the magnetising current is removed.
  • These properties make it suitable for electromagnets and transformer cores.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Soft iron → Electromagnet cores.

Hard magnetic material → Permanent magnets.

16. Magnetic Materials

Magnetic materials are commonly classified as:

  • Diamagnetic.
  • Paramagnetic.
  • Ferromagnetic.
17. Diamagnetic Materials
  • Diamagnetic materials are weakly repelled by a magnetic field.
  • They do not retain permanent magnetisation under ordinary conditions.
  • Examples include bismuth, copper, silver and water.
  • Their magnetic susceptibility is small and negative.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Diamagnetic → Weakly Repelled

18. Paramagnetic Materials
  • Paramagnetic materials are weakly attracted by a magnetic field.
  • Magnetisation disappears largely when the external field is removed.
  • Aluminium is paramagnetic.
  • Platinum is paramagnetic.
  • Oxygen is paramagnetic.
  • Their susceptibility is small and positive.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Paramagnetic → Weakly Attracted

19. Ferromagnetic Materials
  • Ferromagnetic materials are strongly attracted by magnetic fields.
  • They can be strongly magnetised.
  • Iron is ferromagnetic.
  • Cobalt is ferromagnetic.
  • Nickel is ferromagnetic.
  • Ferromagnetism is associated with magnetic domains.
📌 Must-Memorise

Iron → Ferromagnetic

Cobalt → Ferromagnetic

Nickel → Ferromagnetic

20. Magnetic Domains
  • Ferromagnetic materials contain microscopic regions called magnetic domains.
  • Within each domain, many atomic magnetic moments are aligned.
  • In an unmagnetised sample, domains may be oriented in different directions.
  • Magnetisation causes more domains to align with the applied field.
  • Strong alignment produces strong magnetisation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Domain Alignment → Magnetisation

21. Magnetisation
  • Magnetisation is the process of producing magnetic alignment in a material.
  • It may be produced using a magnetic field.
  • Electric current in a coil can magnetise a ferromagnetic core.
  • Mechanical shock or heating can disturb magnetic domain alignment and reduce magnetisation.
22. Demagnetisation
  • Demagnetisation is the loss or reduction of magnetism.
  • Heating can demagnetise magnetic materials.
  • Repeated mechanical shocks may reduce magnetisation.
  • Applying a suitable alternating magnetic field can demagnetise a material.
  • Storage conditions can affect permanent magnets.
23. Curie Temperature
  • Above a characteristic temperature called the Curie temperature, a ferromagnetic material loses its long-range ferromagnetic order.
  • Above the Curie temperature, it becomes paramagnetic.
  • The Curie temperature differs for different materials.
  • The concept is associated with Pierre Curie.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Curie Temperature → Ferromagnetism Lost

24. Retentivity
  • Retentivity is the ability of a magnetic material to retain magnetisation after the external magnetic field is removed.
  • Permanent-magnet materials require high retentivity.
  • Soft magnetic materials generally have lower retained magnetisation in practical use.
25. Coercivity
  • Coercivity measures resistance to demagnetisation.
  • A high-coercivity material requires a strong reverse magnetic field to demagnetise it.
  • Permanent magnets require high coercivity.
  • Transformer-core materials require low coercivity to reduce hysteresis loss.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Permanent Magnet → High Coercivity

Transformer Core → Low Coercivity

26. Magnetic Hysteresis
  • Hysteresis is the lag of magnetisation behind changes in magnetising field.
  • A hysteresis loop shows magnetic response during a complete magnetisation cycle.
  • The area of the hysteresis loop represents energy lost per cycle per unit volume in a magnetic material.
  • Soft magnetic materials have narrow hysteresis loops.
  • Permanent-magnet materials have wider loops.
27. Hysteresis Loss
  • Repeated magnetisation and demagnetisation dissipates energy as heat.
  • This is called hysteresis loss.
  • Transformer cores are made from soft magnetic materials with low hysteresis loss.
  • Silicon steel is widely used in traditional transformer cores.
28. Magnetic Compass
  • A compass contains a small freely rotating magnet.
  • It aligns approximately with Earth's magnetic field.
  • Its north-seeking end points approximately toward geographic north.
  • Compasses were historically important for navigation.
  • Nearby magnets and electric currents can disturb compass readings.
29. Earth as a Magnet
  • Earth possesses a large-scale magnetic field.
  • Earth's field approximately resembles that of a tilted magnetic dipole, though the real field is more complex.
  • A compass aligns with Earth's magnetic field.
  • Earth's magnetic axis is not exactly aligned with its geographic rotation axis.
  • Earth's magnetic field changes slowly with time.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Earth → Giant Magnetic Field → Compass Alignment

30. Geographic and Magnetic Poles
  • Geographic poles are defined by Earth's axis of rotation.
  • Magnetic poles are defined by Earth's magnetic field.
  • Geographic and magnetic poles do not coincide exactly.
  • Magnetic pole positions shift over time.
  • The north-seeking pole of a compass points toward geographic north because that region behaves approximately like a magnetic south pole in elementary dipole terminology.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Geographic North Pole ≠ Exactly same as magnetic pole.

31. Magnetic Meridian
  • Magnetic meridian is the vertical plane containing the direction of Earth's magnetic field at a location.
  • A freely suspended compass needle aligns in the local magnetic meridian.
  • Magnetic meridian may differ from geographic meridian.
32. Magnetic Declination
  • Magnetic declination is the angle between geographic meridian and magnetic meridian.
  • Declination may be east or west.
  • It varies from place to place.
  • It also changes slowly with time.
  • Compass navigation may require correction for magnetic declination.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Declination → Geographic North vs Magnetic North Direction

33. Angle of Dip
  • Angle of dip or magnetic inclination is the angle Earth's magnetic field makes with the horizontal.
  • It is measured in the magnetic meridian.
  • Near the magnetic equator, dip is approximately 0°.
  • Near magnetic poles, dip approaches 90°.
  • A dip needle measures magnetic inclination.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Magnetic Equator → Dip ≈ 0°

Magnetic Poles → Dip ≈ 90°

34. Magnetic Equator
  • Magnetic equator is a line connecting places where magnetic dip is approximately zero.
  • Earth's magnetic field is nearly horizontal there.
  • It does not exactly coincide with geographic equator.
35. Horizontal Component of Earth's Field
  • Earth's magnetic field can be resolved into horizontal and vertical components.
  • Horizontal component is strongest where the field is nearly horizontal.
  • Near the magnetic equator, the horizontal component is relatively large.
  • Near magnetic poles, horizontal component approaches zero because field is nearly vertical.
36. Magnetosphere
  • The magnetosphere is the region around Earth strongly influenced by Earth's magnetic field.
  • It interacts with charged particles from the solar wind.
  • Earth's magnetosphere helps shield the atmosphere and surface from many charged solar particles.
  • The magnetosphere is compressed on the Sun-facing side and stretched into a long tail on the night side.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Magnetosphere → Protection from Solar Wind

37. Aurora
  • Auroras are light displays produced when charged particles interact with gases in Earth's upper atmosphere.
  • Earth's magnetic field guides many charged particles toward polar regions.
  • Aurora Borealis occurs in northern high latitudes.
  • Aurora Australis occurs in southern high latitudes.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Aurora Borealis → North

Aurora Australis → South

38. Magnetic Effect of Electric Current
  • Electric current produces a magnetic field.
  • Hans Christian Oersted demonstrated this connection in 1820.
  • A compass needle deflects near a current-carrying conductor.
  • Oersted's discovery linked electricity and magnetism.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Oersted → 1820 → Current Produces Magnetic Field

39. Magnetic Field Around a Straight Conductor
  • A current-carrying straight wire produces circular magnetic field lines around it.
  • Field direction depends on current direction.
  • Magnetic field becomes weaker with greater distance from the wire.
  • Greater current produces a stronger field.
40. Right-Hand Thumb Rule
  • Right-Hand Thumb Rule gives the direction of magnetic field around a straight current-carrying conductor.
  • Point the right thumb in the direction of conventional current.
  • Curled fingers show direction of magnetic field lines.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Right Thumb → Current

Curled Fingers → Magnetic Field

41. Current into and out of Page
  • A dot symbol can represent a vector coming out of the page.
  • A cross symbol can represent a vector going into the page.
  • These symbols are commonly used for current and magnetic-field directions.
📌 Memory

Dot → Arrow tip → Coming out

Cross → Arrow tail/feathers → Going in

42. Magnetic Field of Circular Coil
  • A current-carrying circular coil produces a magnetic field.
  • At the centre, field lines are nearly parallel over a small region.
  • Increasing current increases field strength.
  • Increasing number of turns increases field strength.
  • Coil direction determines which face behaves as north or south.
43. Clock Rule for a Current Loop
  • Viewed from one face of a current-carrying circular coil:
  • Anticlockwise current makes that face behave like a north pole.
  • Clockwise current makes that face behave like a south pole.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Anticlockwise → North

Clockwise → South

44. Solenoid
  • A solenoid is a long cylindrical coil containing many turns of insulated wire.
  • Current through a solenoid produces a magnetic field.
  • Field inside a long ideal solenoid is nearly uniform.
  • A solenoid behaves magnetically like a bar magnet.
  • One end acts as north and the other as south.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Solenoid → Coil behaving like bar magnet

45. Magnetic Field Inside Solenoid
  • Magnetic field inside a long solenoid is strong and approximately uniform.
  • Outside, the field is weaker.
  • Increasing current increases field.
  • Increasing turns per unit length increases field.
  • Adding a soft-iron core greatly increases field strength.
46. Electromagnet Applications
  • Electric bells.
  • Relays.
  • Electromagnetic cranes.
  • Circuit breakers.
  • Loudspeakers.
  • Electric motors.
  • Magnetic door locks.
  • Some medical and industrial devices.
47. Electromagnetic Crane
  • Electromagnetic cranes lift iron and steel materials.
  • Current through a coil magnetises a soft-iron core.
  • Switching current on allows lifting.
  • Switching current off releases the load.
  • This controllability is an advantage over permanent magnets.
48. Electric Bell
  • An electric bell uses an electromagnet.
  • Current through a coil magnetises an iron core.
  • The electromagnet attracts an armature.
  • The hammer strikes the bell.
  • Circuit interruption causes the electromagnet to release the armature.
  • Repeated make-and-break action produces ringing.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Electric Bell → Electromagnet

49. Relay
  • A relay is an electrically controlled switch.
  • An electromagnet moves contacts.
  • A small control current can switch a separate circuit.
  • Relays provide electrical isolation in many applications.
50. Force on Current-Carrying Conductor
  • A current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field can experience a force.
  • Force magnitude is F = BIL sinθ for a straight conductor in a uniform field.
  • B is magnetic flux density.
  • I is current.
  • L is conductor length in the field.
  • θ is angle between current and magnetic field.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Magnetic Force on Wire → BIL sinθ

51. Maximum and Zero Magnetic Force
  • Force is maximum when current is perpendicular to magnetic field.
  • sin 90° = 1.
  • Force is zero when current is parallel or antiparallel to magnetic field.
  • sin 0° = 0.
📌 Remember

I ⟂ B → Force maximum

I ∥ B → Force zero

52. Fleming's Left-Hand Rule
  • Fleming's Left-Hand Rule gives direction of force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field.
  • Forefinger shows magnetic field.
  • Middle finger shows current.
  • Thumb shows force or motion.
  • The three are mutually perpendicular.
📌 Must-Memorise

Left Hand → Motor

Forefinger → Field

Middle finger → Current

Thumb → Motion/Force

53. Electric Motor
  • An electric motor converts electrical energy into mechanical energy.
  • It works on the force experienced by a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field.
  • A current-carrying coil experiences torque.
  • The coil rotates.
  • DC motors commonly use a split-ring commutator.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Motor → Electrical to Mechanical

54. Split-Ring Commutator
  • A split-ring commutator reverses current direction in a rotating coil every half turn in a simple DC motor.
  • This keeps torque acting in the same overall rotational sense.
  • Carbon brushes maintain electrical contact with the rotating commutator.
55. Motor Applications
  • Electric fans.
  • Mixers.
  • Pumps.
  • Washing machines.
  • Electric vehicles.
  • Industrial machinery.
  • Computer cooling fans.
56. Force on Moving Charge
  • A moving electric charge in a magnetic field can experience magnetic force.
  • F = qvB sinθ in magnitude.
  • q is charge.
  • v is speed.
  • B is magnetic flux density.
  • θ is angle between velocity and magnetic field.
  • Magnetic force is perpendicular to both velocity and magnetic field.
57. Magnetic Force Does No Work on a Point Charge
  • Magnetic force on a moving point charge is perpendicular to velocity.
  • Therefore, an ideal magnetic field changes the direction of velocity but not its speed.
  • The magnetic force alone does no mechanical work on the charged particle.
  • It can produce circular or helical motion.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Magnetic field alone → Changes direction, not kinetic energy.

58. Charged Particle in Uniform Magnetic Field
  • A charged particle moving perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field follows a circular path.
  • Magnetic force acts as centripetal force.
  • Oppositely charged particles curve in opposite directions.
  • If velocity has a component parallel to the field, the particle can follow a helical path.
59. Electromagnetic Induction
  • Electromagnetic induction is production of emf due to change in magnetic flux.
  • Michael Faraday discovered electromagnetic induction.
  • Faraday's major induction experiments were performed in 1831.
  • Moving a magnet relative to a coil can induce current.
  • Changing current in a nearby coil can also induce emf.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Faraday → 1831 → Electromagnetic Induction

60. Faraday's Law
  • Induced emf is proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux linkage.
  • Faster change in magnetic flux produces greater induced emf.
  • Increasing number of coil turns can increase induced emf.
  • Electric generators operate on Faraday's law.
  • Transformers also depend on electromagnetic induction.
61. Lenz's Law
  • Lenz's Law determines direction of induced current.
  • Induced current acts in a direction that opposes the change producing it.
  • Heinrich Lenz formulated the law.
  • Lenz's Law is consistent with conservation of energy.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Lenz → Induced Current Opposes Change

62. Ways to Increase Induced EMF
  • Increase relative speed between magnet and coil.
  • Use a stronger magnetic field.
  • Increase number of turns in coil.
  • Increase rate of change of magnetic flux.
  • Change coil area or orientation more rapidly where applicable.
63. Electric Generator
  • An electric generator converts mechanical energy into electrical energy.
  • It works on electromagnetic induction.
  • Mechanical rotation changes magnetic flux through a coil.
  • This induces emf.
  • Generators are essentially opposite in energy-conversion role to motors.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Generator → Mechanical to Electrical

Motor → Electrical to Mechanical

64. Fleming's Right-Hand Rule
  • Fleming's Right-Hand Rule gives the direction of induced current in a generator.
  • Forefinger shows magnetic field.
  • Thumb shows motion of conductor.
  • Middle finger shows induced current.
📌 Must-Memorise

Right Hand → Generator

Thumb → Motion

Forefinger → Field

Middle finger → Current

65. Left vs Right Hand Rule
  • Fleming Left-Hand Rule → Motor.
  • Fleming Right-Hand Rule → Generator.
  • Left hand gives force/motion from current and magnetic field.
  • Right hand gives induced current from motion in a magnetic field.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Left → Motor

Right → Generator

66. AC Generator
  • An AC generator produces alternating current.
  • A rotating coil in a magnetic field produces changing emf.
  • Slip rings are used in a simple AC generator.
  • Output reverses direction periodically.
67. DC Generator — Basic Idea
  • A DC generator uses a split-ring commutator in the simplified model.
  • The commutator rectifies the internally alternating emf into a unidirectional output.
  • Practical DC machines can have more complex commutator arrangements.
68. Slip Rings vs Split Rings
  • Slip rings are used in a simple AC generator.
  • Split-ring commutator is associated with simple DC motors and DC generators.
  • Slip rings maintain continuous connection without reversing coil terminals.
  • Split ring reverses connection every half turn.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Slip Ring → AC Generator

Split Ring → DC Motor

69. Transformer
  • A transformer changes alternating voltage.
  • It works on mutual electromagnetic induction.
  • It contains primary and secondary coils.
  • Both coils are usually wound around a magnetic core.
  • AC in the primary produces changing magnetic flux.
  • Changing flux induces emf in the secondary.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Transformer → Mutual Induction → AC

70. Step-Up Transformer
  • A step-up transformer increases voltage.
  • Secondary coil has more turns than primary in the ideal case.
  • Vs/Vp = Ns/Np.
  • If voltage increases in an ideal transformer, current decreases correspondingly for approximately constant power.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Step-Up → Ns > Np → Voltage ↑

71. Step-Down Transformer
  • A step-down transformer decreases voltage.
  • Secondary coil has fewer turns than primary.
  • Ns < Np.
  • Step-down transformers are used in adapters and distribution systems.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Step-Down → Ns < Np → Voltage ↓

72. Transformer Equation

For an ideal transformer:

  • Vs/Vp = Ns/Np.
  • V is voltage.
  • N is number of turns.
  • Primary is input coil.
  • Secondary is output coil.
📌 Remember

Voltage Ratio = Turns Ratio

73. Why Transformer Requires AC
  • A transformer requires changing magnetic flux.
  • AC continuously changes current and magnetic flux.
  • Steady DC produces no continuously changing flux after the initial switching transient.
  • Therefore, ordinary transformers do not continuously transform steady DC.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Transformer → AC, not steady DC.

74. Transformer Core
  • Transformer cores are made from soft magnetic material.
  • High magnetic permeability improves flux linkage.
  • Low coercivity reduces hysteresis loss.
  • Laminated cores reduce eddy-current loss.
  • Silicon steel has traditionally been used in many power transformers.
75. Eddy Currents
  • Eddy currents are circulating currents induced in bulk conductors by changing magnetic fields.
  • Eddy currents cause heating.
  • Transformer cores are laminated to reduce eddy currents.
  • Eddy currents are deliberately used in induction heating and electromagnetic braking.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Lamination → Eddy Current Loss ↓

76. Electromagnetic Braking
  • Eddy currents can produce magnetic forces opposing motion.
  • This principle is used in some trains, amusement rides and measuring instruments.
  • Electromagnetic braking can reduce mechanical contact and wear.
77. Induction Heating
  • Alternating magnetic fields induce eddy currents in conducting materials.
  • Electrical resistance converts these currents into heat.
  • Induction cooktops use electromagnetic induction to heat suitable cookware.
  • Ferromagnetic cookware is especially effective in many induction systems.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Induction Cooker → Electromagnetic Induction + Eddy Current Heating

78. Induction Cooker
  • A coil beneath the cooking surface carries alternating current.
  • It produces a changing magnetic field.
  • The field induces currents in compatible cookware.
  • Resistance and magnetic losses generate heat in the vessel.
  • The cooking vessel itself is heated directly.
79. Loudspeaker
  • A loudspeaker converts electrical signals into sound.
  • A current-carrying voice coil interacts with a permanent magnetic field.
  • Magnetic force moves the coil.
  • The attached cone vibrates.
  • Vibrating cone produces sound waves.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Loudspeaker → Electrical to Mechanical to Sound

80. Microphone — Electromagnetic Type
  • A dynamic microphone converts sound-induced mechanical vibration into electrical signals.
  • A coil moves relative to a magnetic field.
  • Electromagnetic induction produces an electrical signal.
  • It performs the reverse transduction role of a loudspeaker in basic comparison.
81. Galvanometer
  • A moving-coil galvanometer detects and measures small electric currents.
  • It works on torque experienced by a current-carrying coil in a magnetic field.
  • The coil rotates against a restoring torque.
  • Deflection can be related to current.
82. Ammeter and Voltmeter Link
  • A galvanometer can be converted into an ammeter using a low-resistance shunt.
  • A galvanometer can be converted into a voltmeter using a high resistance in series.
  • Magnetic effects of current are used in traditional analog meters.
83. Magnetic Recording
  • Magnetic materials can store information through magnetised regions.
  • Traditional magnetic tapes use magnetisable coatings.
  • Hard disk drives store information magnetically.
  • Read/write heads alter and detect magnetic patterns.
84. Magnetic Stripe
  • Magnetic stripes on older cards store encoded magnetic information.
  • A reader detects changes in magnetisation.
  • Magnetic-stripe technology has been widely used in identification and payment cards.
85. MRI — Basic Magnetic Link
  • MRI stands for Magnetic Resonance Imaging.
  • MRI uses strong magnetic fields and radiofrequency pulses.
  • It primarily detects signals associated with hydrogen nuclei in the body.
  • MRI does not use ionising X-rays for image formation.
  • Strong magnetic fields require strict safety precautions around ferromagnetic objects.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

MRI → Strong Magnet + Radio Waves

86. Magnetic Levitation
  • Magnetic levitation uses magnetic forces to support or guide objects without ordinary mechanical contact.
  • Maglev trains use magnetic forces for levitation and propulsion.
  • Reduced contact can greatly reduce rolling friction.
  • Different maglev technologies use electromagnets or superconducting systems.
87. Earth Dynamo
  • Earth's magnetic field is generated mainly by motion of electrically conducting molten iron-rich fluid in the outer core.
  • Convection and Earth's rotation contribute to the geodynamo.
  • Earth's magnetic field can reverse polarity over geological time.
  • These reversals are recorded in magnetic minerals in rocks.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Earth's Field Source → Outer-Core Geodynamo

88. Paleomagnetism
  • Paleomagnetism is the study of ancient magnetic fields recorded in rocks.
  • Magnetic minerals can preserve the direction of Earth's field when rocks form.
  • Paleomagnetic evidence strongly supported plate tectonics and seafloor spreading.
  • Symmetrical magnetic stripes occur on either side of mid-ocean ridges.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Paleomagnetism → Evidence for Seafloor Spreading

89. Magnetic Reversals
  • Earth's magnetic polarity has reversed many times in geological history.
  • During reversal, magnetic north and south orientations switch.
  • Reversals are recorded in rocks.
  • Magnetic reversals are irregular rather than occurring at fixed intervals.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Geomagnetic reversals do not occur on a fixed regular schedule.

90. Oersted
  • Hans Christian Oersted was a Danish physicist.
  • In 1820, he observed that electric current deflects a compass needle.
  • His discovery demonstrated that electricity produces magnetism.
  • It helped launch the field of electromagnetism.
91. André-Marie Ampère
  • Ampère developed mathematical descriptions of forces involving electric currents.
  • He made major contributions to electrodynamics.
  • The SI unit of electric current, ampere, is named after him.
  • Ampère's work followed Oersted's discovery.
92. Michael Faraday
  • Michael Faraday discovered electromagnetic induction.
  • His major induction work dates to 1831.
  • He introduced important concepts involving electric and magnetic fields.
  • Faraday's work made practical generators and transformers possible.
  • The unit farad is named after him.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Faraday → Induction → 1831

93. Heinrich Lenz
  • Heinrich Lenz formulated Lenz's Law.
  • Lenz's Law gives direction of induced current.
  • Induced effects oppose the change producing them.
  • His law supports conservation of energy.
94. James Clerk Maxwell
  • James Clerk Maxwell unified electricity and magnetism mathematically.
  • Maxwell's equations describe classical electromagnetism.
  • Maxwell showed that light is an electromagnetic wave.
  • His work predicted electromagnetic waves travelling at the speed of light.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Maxwell → Unified Electricity + Magnetism → Light is EM Wave

95. Nikola Tesla
  • Nikola Tesla made major contributions to alternating-current electrical systems.
  • The SI unit tesla is named after him.
  • Tesla worked on AC motors and polyphase power systems.
  • He is strongly associated with development of practical AC technology.
96. William Gilbert
  • William Gilbert made important early scientific studies of magnetism.
  • His work De Magnete was published in 1600.
  • Gilbert proposed that Earth behaves like a giant magnet.
  • He is often regarded as an early pioneer of experimental magnetism.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

William Gilbert → De Magnete → 1600 → Earth as Magnet

97. Pierre Curie
  • Pierre Curie studied magnetic properties of materials.
  • Curie's Law describes temperature dependence of paramagnetism under suitable conditions.
  • Curie temperature is named in connection with magnetic phase transitions.
  • Pierre Curie shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with Marie Curie and Henri Becquerel for work related to radioactivity.

  • Magnetic field strength H → Ampere per metre.
  • Magnetic moment → A m² in SI.
  • Electric current → Ampere.

  • Magnetic flux → Φ = BA cosθ.
  • Force on current-carrying conductor → F = BIL sinθ.
  • Force on moving charge → F = qvB sinθ.
  • Transformer ratio → Vs/Vp = Ns/Np.
  • Magnetic flux density unit relation → 1 T = 1 Wb/m².
